rubric.why: Identifies the source of nuclear energy.
rubric.description: Energy comes from the nucleus of an atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the energy originates in the atomic nucleus.

rubric.why: Explains how nuclear energy is obtained.
rubric.description: Energy is released during a nuclear reaction, such as fission or fusion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that nuclear energy is released in a nuclear reaction.

modelAnswer: Nuclear energy is the energy stored in the nucleus of an atom.
It is released during nuclear reactions such as fission or fusion.

items.followUp: Define work and write its SI unit.

rubric.why: States the defining relationship for pressure.
rubric.description: Pressure is force acting per unit area.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition of pressure.

rubric.why: Identifies the SI unit of pressure.
rubric.description: The SI unit is the pascal (Pa), equal to one newton per square metre.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for pascal or its equivalent unit.

modelAnswer: Pressure is the force acting per unit area of a surface.
Its SI unit is the pascal (Pa).
1 Pa = 1 N m⁻².

items.followUp: State two differences between solids and liquids.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the shapes of liquids and gases.
rubric.description: A liquid has a fixed volume but no fixed shape; a gas has neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct difference involving shape or volume.

rubric.why: Distinguishes how liquids and gases respond to compression.
rubric.description: Liquids are almost incompressible, whereas gases are highly compressible.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly contrasting their compressibility.

modelAnswer: A liquid has a fixed volume but no fixed shape; it takes the shape of its container.
A gas has neither a fixed volume nor a fixed shape and fills its container.
Liquids are almost incompressible, whereas gases are highly compressible.

items.followUp: Use Newton’s second law to find the force needed to accelerate a 4 kg body at 3 m s⁻².

rubric.why: States Newton’s second law in words.
rubric.description: The rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force and occurs in the direction of that force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct law in words.

rubric.why: Relates force to the change in momentum or to mass and acceleration.
rubric.description: For constant mass, F = Δp/Δt = ma.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for deriving or stating the mathematical form.

rubric.why: Connects the force equation to the unit newton.
rubric.description: For a 1 kg mass accelerating at 1 m s⁻², the force is 1 N.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the unit force from F = ma.

rubric.why: Defines the SI unit of force.
rubric.description: One newton is the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m s⁻²; 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻².
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition or equivalent unit.

modelAnswer: Newton’s second law states that the rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction of that force.
For a body of mass m, initial velocity u and final velocity v reached in time t:
Change in momentum = mv − mu = m(v − u).
Rate of change of momentum = m(v − u)/t = ma.
Therefore, F = ma.
For m = 1 kg and a = 1 m s⁻², F = 1 × 1 = 1 N.
Thus, one newton is the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m s⁻²; 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻².

items.followUp: A room measures 6 m × 4 m × 3 m. If the density of air is 1.2 kg m⁻³, find the mass of air in the room.

rubric.why: Records the given density in SI units.
rubric.description: Density of air, ρ = 1.3 kg m⁻³.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying the density.

rubric.why: Uses the room dimensions to find its volume.
rubric.description: The room dimensions are 8 m, 5 m and 4 m.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying the dimensions.

rubric.why: Calculates the room’s volume.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct volume with units.

rubric.why: Selects the density relationship for mass.
rubric.description: m = ρV.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula.

rubric.why: Substitutes and obtains the mass with units.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct final mass.

modelAnswer: Given: ρ = 1.3 kg m⁻³; l = 8 m; b = 5 m; h = 4 m.
Volume of room: V = lbh.
Formula: ρ = m/V, so m = ρV.
Mass of air in the room = 208 kg.

rubric.description: Any two correct branches of physics.
rubric.how: Award ½ mark for each correct branch, up to 1 mark.

rubric.why: Credits additional correct names of branches of physics.

rubric.how: Award ½ mark for each additional correct branch, up to 1 mark.

modelAnswer: Four main branches of physics are mechanics, heat, sound and light.

items.followUp: Name the three types of motion and give one example of each.

rubric.why: Identifies translatory motion as a type of motion.
rubric.description: Translatory motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming translatory (translational) motion.

rubric.why: Identifies the other two types of motion.
rubric.description: Rotatory and vibratory motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both remaining types.

modelAnswer: The three types of motion are translatory motion, rotatory motion and vibratory motion.

items.followUp: State Newton’s third law of motion.

rubric.why: States what happens to a body when the resultant external force is zero.
rubric.description: A body remains at rest or continues moving with uniform velocity in a straight line unless acted upon by a resultant external force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct statement of the first law, including the condition of no resultant external force.

rubric.why: Shows understanding of the law’s connection to inertia.
rubric.description: This tendency to resist a change in its state of rest or motion is called inertia.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the tendency as inertia or correctly explaining resistance to a change in motion.

modelAnswer: Newton’s first law states that a body remains at rest or continues to move with uniform velocity in a straight line unless acted upon by a resultant external force.
This tendency to resist a change in its state of rest or motion is called inertia.
